image_description: An underwater photograph showing a large marine mammal, identified as a sea lion, swimming diagonally from the upper left to the lower right. The animal has a streamlined, fusiform body with dark grey/brown fur that appears lighter on the ventral side due to lighting. It is positioned against a backdrop of dark, textured rock formations and blue water with visible particulate matter. A diver is faintly visible in the background on the right.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is visible but appears relatively smooth without a pronounced sagittal crest, suggesting this may be a female or juvenile, or the angle obscures the feature. It does not clearly match the 'prominent crest' description.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: A small, distinct external ear flap is visible on the side of the head, confirming it is an eared seal (sea lion/fur seal) and not a true seal.
Faint but visible whisker follicles/whiskers can be seen on the snout area, consistent with pinniped anatomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreflipper is visible, appearing large and broad. While the 'hairless underside' is hard to verify definitively underwater, the general morphology matches.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The hind flipper is visible at the rear. While its rotation capability isn't demonstrated in a static swim pose, the structure is present and anatomically consistent with otariids.
Despite the angled perspective, the visible portions of the body suggest standard bilateral symmetry without obvious deformities.
